Arlington website design for the crowd and the neighbors

Some customers come for one game. Others live five minutes away. A good site talks to both, and you can see yours free before paying.

Arlington website design has an unusual job. The same city that fills a stadium on Sunday afternoon is, on Tuesday morning, a place of around 400,000 people who need a dentist, a brake job or a birthday cake. A business here can live on both kinds of customer, and its site has to make sense to each of them within a few seconds on a phone.

To be clear up front, this page is about Arlington, Texas, the city between Dallas and Fort Worth. Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson, a Texan who builds every site by hand from Big Sandy in East Texas. You see a free demo first, and the price is printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time.

Two customers, one address

The visitor on event day

Arlington's entertainment district holds AT&T Stadium, Globe Life Field, Six Flags Over Texas and Texas Live!. Those venues draw visitors from well beyond the city, and most of them do not know the streets. They search on a phone for food, a place to wait out traffic or a fix for a flat, and they choose fast.

The neighbor all year

The 2020 census counted 394,266 residents, making Arlington the second largest city in Tarrant County. UT Arlington adds tens of thousands of students. These are the customers who come back, leave reviews and tell their friends, and they want to know if you are close, what you charge and when you are open.

Most small businesses do not need two websites for this. They need one site with a clear home page, real hours and a service or menu page written in plain words, plus a short note for event days when something changes.

Web design for Arlington, TX customers who mostly drive

Arlington has long been known as a large city without fixed-route buses. In their place, the city runs an on-demand rideshare service with Via: riders book by app or phone and get picked up within a couple of blocks, and the service has added links to regional rail at the CentrePort TRE station. For most customers, though, getting to you means a car, a freeway and a parking spot.

That changes what a site should say. Name the nearest highway exit or big cross street, like Cooper Street at I-20 by The Parks Mall, mention parking, and keep the tap-to-call number at the top of every page. Someone coming from Grand Prairie or Mansfield wants to know the trip is worth it before they leave.

It matters for search as well. Google says distance is one of the three main things behind its local results, along with relevance and prominence, so a page that says exactly where in Arlington you are gives it something solid to work with.

A short game-day checklist for your site

If big events touch your business at all, a few small things on the website prevent a lot of missed sales and annoyed phone calls:

  • Event-day hours, written as text on the home page, not buried in a social media post.
  • A line on whether you are inside the event traffic area, and the best way in.
  • Your menu, price list or services as real text that loads quickly on a weak signal.
  • One button to call and one to get directions, both visible without scrolling.
  • A plain note when you are closed for an event, so nobody drives over for nothing.

Help for Arlington owners from the city, the chamber and the SBDC

The website is one piece of running a business here. These local programs cover a lot of the rest:

  • Arlington Economic Development CorporationHas worked with partners such as LiftFund on small business lending and with SCORE on mentoring programs. Check its site for what is open now.
  • City of ArlingtonIts small business assistance pages cover first steps, financing and how to sell to the city.
  • Greater Arlington Chamber of CommerceHosts small business events, including a Small Business Expo, and recognizes member businesses through its small business awards.
  • Tarrant Small Business Development CenterFree one-on-one advising for owners across Tarrant County, Arlington included.

Common questions

How much does Arlington website design cost for a small business?

It depends on who you hire and what is included, so ask for the first-year total in writing. Ours is printed: Starter is $497 for five pages, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten city pages, and Agency is $1,997 for a researched page for each town and service worth having, each paid once. Hosting, maintenance and updates cost $49 a month, or nothing extra while you keep the AI agent.

Is Arlington close to Dallas?

Yes. Arlington sits between Dallas and Fort Worth in Tarrant County, roughly 20 miles west of downtown Dallas and about 12 miles east of downtown Fort Worth. That middle position is why an Arlington business can draw customers from both directions, and why its website should say which side of the city it is on and how people get there.

Is there a web design company in Arlington, TX that shows the site first?

We build a free demo for your business before you pay anything, though we are not based in Arlington. Maurice Johnson writes and builds each site from Big Sandy in East Texas and works with you by phone, email and shared links. Call (903) 636-7511 any hour; an AI receptionist answers and can transfer you to Maurice.

Do you do web design in Arlington, Virginia too?

We can build for a business anywhere in the country, but this page is about Arlington, Texas, in Tarrant County. If you are in Virginia, the packages and the free demo are the same; the local research would simply be about your Arlington instead.

Should my site show different hours on event days?

If your hours or your parking change when there is a game or a concert, yes. Put a short note on the home page and the contact page, keep it current, and say plainly whether you are open early or closed. Visitors who drove in from the other side of the Metroplex will thank you for not making them guess.
